lesson.title: BSS: The Basic Building Block of Wi-Fi
lesson.summary: A Basic Service Set is one access point together with every client currently associated with it, forming the smallest self-contained unit of a Wi-Fi network that every larger deployment is built from.
lesson.body:
Every wireless LAN, no matter how large, is assembled from a smallest working unit, just as a wired LAN can be described in terms of individual switches before considering how many are cabled together. In Wi-Fi terminology that smallest unit is the Basic Service Set, or BSS: one access point plus the complete set of client stations currently associated with it, all sharing the same channel and the same SSID, and all following that access point's coordination for who transmits when.

Every BSS has a unique identifier called the BSSID, and in the overwhelmingly common infrastructure case, the BSSID is simply the MAC address of the access point's radio. This matters because the SSID alone is not enough to distinguish between access points; several access points can legitimately broadcast the identical SSID, as in the library example from the SSID concept, but each one still has its own distinct BSSID, letting client software tell them apart while presenting a single network name to the user.

The standard also defines an Independent BSS, or IBSS, sometimes called ad hoc mode, where client stations communicate directly with each other with no access point at all. This is rare in practice today, mostly replaced by Wi-Fi Direct and Bluetooth for direct device to device use cases, but it illustrates that the defining feature of a BSS is the group of stations coordinating over one shared channel, not the specific presence of an access point. The far more common case, worth focusing on, is the infrastructure BSS built around an access point as described above, where the access point is not just a member of the group but the coordinator every other station depends on to reach the rest of the network at all.

Picture a small studio apartment with one Wi-Fi router and four devices connected to it: a phone, a laptop, a smart TV, and a printer. That router's access point, together with those four associated devices, forms exactly one BSS. All four devices contend for airtime on the same channel using the collision avoidance rules from the wireless LAN concept, and all four are represented within the network by the single BSSID, the router's MAC address, even though each device also keeps its own individual MAC address for identifying itself within the BSS.

A BSS works well for a single room or a small home, but it has an inherent limit: an access point's radio only reaches so far, so a large office or campus needs multiple access points to cover the whole space, and a person walking from one end of the building to the other needs to stay connected the entire time. A single BSS by itself has no built-in way to hand a client off to a neighboring access point; as far as one BSS is concerned, a client that leaves its radio range has simply disconnected. Stitching multiple BSSs together into one seamless network that a client can roam across is exactly the problem the next concept, the Extended Service Set, is built to solve.
